claims.text: Location: in the thoracic cavity between the lungs, in the mediastinum.
claims.quote: The human heart is located within the thoracic cavity, medially between the lungs in the space known as the mediastinum.

claims.text: Pericardium: a sturdy outer fibrous layer and an inner serous layer.
claims.quote: The pericardium, which literally translates as “around the heart,” consists of two distinct sublayers: the sturdy outer fibrous pericardium and the inner serous pericardium.

claims.text: Serous pericardium: a parietal layer fused to the fibrous pericardium and a visceral layer (epicardium) fused to the heart; the pericardial cavity between them holds serous fluid.
claims.quote: The more delicate serous pericardium consists of two layers: the parietal pericardium, which is fused to the fibrous pericardium, and an inner visceral pericardium, or epicardium, which is fused to the heart and is part of the heart wall. The pericardial cavity, filled with lubricating serous fluid, lies between the epicardium and the pericardium.

claims.text: Right atrium: receives the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus.
claims.quote: The two major systemic veins, the superior and inferior venae cavae, and the large coronary vein called the coronary sinus that drains the heart myocardium empty into the right atrium.

claims.text: Tricuspid and mitral: tricuspid on the right and mitral on the left, both attached to papillary muscles by chordae tendineae.
claims.quote: papillary muscles attached to the tricuspid valve on the right as well as the mitral valve on the left via chordae tendineae.

claims.text: Pulmonary valve: at the base of the pulmonary trunk; prevents backflow from it.
claims.quote: At the base of the pulmonary trunk is the pulmonary semilunar valve that prevents backflow from the pulmonary trunk.

claims.text: Aortic valve: at the base of the aorta; prevents backflow from it.
claims.quote: At the base of the aorta is the aortic semilunar valve, or the aortic valve, which prevents backflow from the aorta.

claims.text: Semilunar valves: have no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles.
claims.quote: The aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves lack the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles associated with the atrioventricular valves.

claims.text: Most common valve disorder: mitral regurgitation, in about 2 percent of the population; the pulmonary valve is the least often involved.
claims.quote: While any of the heart valves may be involved in valve disorders, mitral regurgitation is the most common, detected in approximately 2 percent of the population, and the pulmonary semilunar valve is the least frequently involved.

claims.text: Coronary origins: the coronary arteries are the first branches of the ascending aorta, arising from aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve.
claims.quote: The first vessels that branch from the ascending aorta are the paired coronary arteries (see Figure 20.25), which arise from two of the three sinuses in the ascending aorta just superior to the aortic semilunar valve.

claims.text: Left coronary artery: supplies the left atrium, left ventricle and interventricular septum; its branches are the circumflex (along the coronary sulcus to the left) and the anterior interventricular artery (LAD).
claims.quote: The left coronary artery distributes blood to the left side of the heart, the left atrium and ventricle, and the interventricular septum. The circumflex artery arises from the left coronary artery and follows the coronary sulcus to the left. Eventually, it will fuse with the small branches of the right coronary artery. The larger anterior interventricular artery, also known as the left anterior descending artery (LAD), is the second major branch arising from the left coronary artery.

claims.text: Right coronary artery: supplies the right atrium, parts of both ventricles and the conduction system; it gives the marginal arteries and, posteriorly, the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery.
claims.quote: The right coronary artery proceeds along the coronary sulcus and distributes blood to the right atrium, portions of both ventricles, and the heart conduction system. Normally, one or more marginal arteries arise from the right coronary artery inferior to the right atrium. The marginal arteries supply blood to the superficial portions of the right ventricle. On the posterior surface of the heart, the right coronary artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery, also known as the posterior descending artery.
